1.text: THE CAMP OF THE REINDEER CHUKCHEE. — The camp among the Rein-

2.text: deer Chukchee, and the village among the Maritime Chukchee, form the unit

3.text: of social life. Though unstable, these exist without interruption. The Chuk-

4.text: chee camp is very small. It includes usually two or three families, and the

5.text: whole number of inhabitants is ten or fifteen. Camps of four, five, or six

6.text: families form but a slight minority; and a camp with ten houses is almost

7.text: impossible unless formed for special reasons, like the temporary camps in

8.text: trading-places. As stated before, the number of tents corresponds to the

9.text: number of families, since each family has a house of its own. In most cases

10.text: the camp consists of related families, — for instance, of brothers, cousins,

11.text: etc., with their wives and children. Especially is this the case among people

12.text: of moderate circumstances, where the herds are not so large as to make it

13.text: necessary to keep them apart. When the herd left after the death of the

14.text: father contains no more than a few hundred heads, there is every reason why

15.text: the sons should not divide it into small parts, but should keep it together,

16.text: as before. Among the poorer people, who count their reindeer only by scores,

17.text: the sons are inclined to separate, and to seek a new fortune, each on his

18.text: own account. On the other hand, such small reindeer-owners often join for

19.text: a while with others of similar circumstances, even though not related. “Poor

20.text: people are careless of ties of relationship,” say the Chukchee. Five, and even

21.text: eight, of such poor people, may keep together for a while, join the few reindeer

22.text: they possess in order to form a herd of decent size, spend a couple of months

23.text: in the common camp, and then disperse just as easily as they had joined.

24.text: On the other hand, people who are rich in reindeer have a constant tendency

25.text: to divide the herd and to form two or more separate camps. Moreover, the

26.text: wealthy reindeer-owners are often unable to keep their reindeer well under

27.text: the supervision of their own family alone, and have need of assistants. These

28.text: assistants may be either some distant relatives or poor strangers; so that the

29.text: camp of a rich man may be formed of a family of owners and of one or

30.text: two families of assistants dependent on the master.

31.text: The Master of the Camp. — The master of the camp, who lives in the

32.text: chief house, is called aunraˊlɪn, which means here “one of the chief house;”¹

33.text: also eˊrmečɪn (“the strongest one”) and aᵋttooraˊlɪn (“one of the front house”).

34.text: The inhabitants of the other tents are called nɪm-tuˊmg̣ɪt (pl. of nɪm-tuˊmg̣ɪn,

35.text: “camp-companion,” “camp-neighbor”); also yaarraˊlɪn (“that of the rear house”).
